nodes.name: Knuth's five-guess strategy for 4-position 6-color Mastermind
nodes.statement: For the original 4-position 6-color version, \ifLongCites{\cite{Knuth77}}{Knuth~\cite{Knuth77}} has given a deterministic strategy that wins the game in at most five guesses.
assumptions: For the original 4-position 6-color version
conclusions: has given a deterministic strategy that wins the game in at most five guesses

nodes.name: Knuth: no deterministic 4-round guarantee
nodes.statement: He also showed that no deterministic strategy has a 4-round guarantee.
conclusions: no deterministic strategy has a 4-round guarantee

nodes.name: Information-theoretic lower bound (Duchet)
nodes.statement: He noted that a simple information-theoretic argument (attributed to Pierre Duchet) provides a lower bound of $\Omega(n \log k / \log n)$ for any $k=k(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Any Mastermind strategy needs $\Omega(n\log k/\log n)$ guesses.
assumptions: for any $k=k(n)$
conclusions: a lower bound of $\Omega(n \log k / \log n)$

nodes.name: Chvatal's random guessing theorem
nodes.statement: Extending the result\ifLongCites{~\cite{Erd63}}{~\cite{Erd63} of Erd\H os and R\'enyi} from $k=2$ to larger numbers of colors, he then showed that for any fixed ${\varepsilon} > 0$, $n$ sufficiently large and $k \le n^{1-{\varepsilon}}$, repeatedly asking random guesses until all but the secret code are excluded by the answers is an optimal Codebreaker strategy (up to constant factors). More specifically, using the probabilistic method and random guesses, he showed the existence of a \emph{deterministic non-adaptive} strategy for Codebreaker, that is, a set of $(2+{\varepsilon}) n \frac{1+2 \log k}{\log (n/k)}$ guesses such that the answers uniquely determine any secret code Codemaker might have chosen (here and in the remainder, $\log n$ denotes the binary logarithm of $n$). These bounds hold even in the black-pegs only version of the game.
nodes.statement_short: For $k\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$, random guessing is optimal up to constants; some $(2+\varepsilon)n\frac{1+2\log k}{\log(n/k)}$ non-adaptive guesses determine any code.
assumptions: for any fixed ${\varepsilon} > 0$, $n$ sufficiently large and $k \le n^{1-{\varepsilon}}$
conclusions: repeatedly asking random guesses until all but the secret code are excluded by the answers is an optimal Codebreaker strategy (up to constant factors)

nodes.name: Chvatal's adaptive strategy with $2n\log k+4n$ guesses
nodes.statement: For $k$ between $n$ and $n^2$, Chv\'atal presented a deterministic adaptive strategy using $2n \log k +4n$ guesses. For $k = n$, this strategy does not need white answer-pegs.
assumptions: For $k$ between $n$ and $n^2$
conclusions: a deterministic adaptive strategy using $2n \log k +4n$ guesses

nodes.name: Chen-Cunha-Homer upper bound
nodes.statement: \ifLongCites{\cite{Chen96}}{Chen, Cunha, and Homer~\cite{Chen96}} showed that for any $k \geq n$, $2n \lceil \log n \rceil+2n+\lceil k/n \rceil+2$ guesses suffice.
assumptions: for any $k \geq n$
conclusions: $2n \lceil \log n \rceil+2n+\lceil k/n \rceil+2$ guesses suffice

nodes.name: Goodrich's black-peg upper bound
nodes.statement: \ifLongCites{\cite{Goodrich09}}{Goodrich~\cite{Goodrich09}} proved an upper bound of $n \lceil \log k \rceil +\lceil(2-1/k)n\rceil+k$ for the number of guesses needed to win the Mastermind game with an arbitrary number $k$ of colors and black answer-pegs only.
assumptions: an arbitrary number $k$ of colors and black answer-pegs only
conclusions: an upper bound of $n \lceil \log k \rceil +\lceil(2-1/k)n\rceil+k$ for the number of guesses

nodes.name: Jaeger-Peczarski upper bound
nodes.statement: This was again improved by \ifLongCites{\cite{JaegerP11}}{J\"ager and Peczarski~\cite{JaegerP11}}, who showed an upper bound of $n \lceil \log n \rceil - n + k + 1$ for the case $k > n$ and $n \lceil \log k \rceil + k$ for the case $k \le n$.
conclusions: an upper bound of $n \lceil \log n \rceil - n + k + 1$ for the case $k > n$ and $n \lceil \log k \rceil + k$ for the case $k \le n$

nodes.name: Color set $[k]$
nodes.statement: For a precise description of this game, let us denote by $[k]$ the set $\{1, \ldots, k \}$ of positive integers not exceeding $k$.

nodes.name: Secret code
nodes.statement: At the start of the game, Codemaker chooses a secret code $z \in [k]^n$.

nodes.name: Guess
nodes.statement: In each round, Codebreaker guesses a string $x \in [k]^n$.

nodes.name: Black-peg answer $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$
nodes.statement: Codemaker replies with the numbers $\mathrm{eq}(z,x):= |\{ i \in [n] \mid z_i=x_i\}|$ of positions in which her and Codebreaker's string coincide, and with $\pi(z,x)$, the number of additional pegs having the right color, but being in the wrong position.
nodes.statement_short: The answer to a guess: the number $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$ of exact matches and the number $\pi(z,x)$ of extra right-color wrong-position pegs.

nodes.name: White-peg answer $\pi(z,x)$
nodes.statement: Formally, $\pi(z,x):=\max_{\rho \in S_n}|\{i \in [n] \mid z_{i}=x_{\rho(i)}\}|-\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$, where $S_n$ denotes the set of all permutations of the set $[n]$. In the original game, $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$ is indicated by black answer-pegs, and $\pi(z,x)$ is indicated by white answer-pegs.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi(z,x)$ is the maximum number of matches over permutations of $x$ minus $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$; black pegs show eq, white pegs show $\pi$.

nodes.name: Winning condition
nodes.statement: Based on this and all previous answers, Codebreaker may choose his next guess. He ``wins'' the game if his guess equals Codemaker's secret code.

nodes.name: Black-pegs only Mastermind
nodes.statement: We should note that often, and partially also in this work, a black-pegs only variant is studied, in which Codemaker reveals $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$ but not $\pi(z,x)$.

nodes.name: NP-hardness of Mastermind consistency (Stuckman-Zhang)
nodes.statement: \ifLongCites{\cite{StuckmanZ06}}{Stuckman and Zhang~\cite{StuckmanZ06}} showed that it is NP-hard to decide whether there exists a secret code consistent with a given sequence of queries and black- and white-peg answers.
conclusions: it is NP-hard to decide whether there exists a secret code consistent with a given sequence of queries and black- and white-peg answers

nodes.name: NP-hardness of black-peg Mastermind consistency (Goodrich)
nodes.statement: This result was extended to black-peg Mastermind by Goodrich~\cite{Goodrich09}.
conclusions: This result was extended to black-peg Mastermind

nodes.name: Viglietta: hardness for two colors
nodes.statement: More recently, \ifLongCites{\cite{Viglietta12}}{Viglietta~\cite{Viglietta12}} showed that both hardness results apply also to the setting with only $k=2$ colors.
conclusions: both hardness results apply also to the setting with only $k=2$ colors

nodes.name: Viglietta: counting consistent codes is #P-complete
nodes.statement: In addition, he proved that \emph{counting} the number of consistent secret codes is $\#$P-complete.
conclusions: \emph{counting} the number of consistent secret codes is $\#$P-complete

nodes.name: Koyama-Lai average-case optimal strategy
nodes.statement: \ifLongCites{\cite{KoyamaL93}}{Koyama and Lai~\cite{KoyamaL93}} studied the average-case difficulty of Mastermind. They gave a strategy that solves Mastermind in an expected number of about 4.34 guesses if the secret string is sampled uniformly at random from all $6^4$ possibilities, and they showed that this strategy is optimal.
assumptions: if the secret string is sampled uniformly at random from all $6^4$ possibilities
conclusions: a strategy that solves Mastermind in an expected number of about 4.34 guesses
this strategy is optimal

nodes.name: Memory-restricted Mastermind in $O(n/\log n)$ guesses
nodes.statement: This inspired, among others, the result~\cite{DoerrW12} showing that a memory-restricted version of Mastermind (using only two rows of the board) can still be solved in $O(n / \log n)$ guesses when the number of colors is constant.
assumptions: when the number of colors is constant
conclusions: a memory-restricted version of Mastermind (using only two rows of the board) can still be solved in $O(n / \log n)$ guesses

nodes.name: Main theorem: adaptive black-peg strategy with $O(n\log\log n + k)$ guesses
nodes.statement: For Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k=k(n)$ colors, the following holds. \begin{itemize} \item If $k= \Omega(n)$ then there exists a randomized winning strategy that uses black pegs only and needs an expected number of $O(n \log \log n + k)$ guesses. \item If $k= o(n)$ then there exists a randomized winning strategy that uses black pegs only and needs an expected number of $O\left(n \log \left(\frac{\log n}{\log (n/k)}\right)\right)$ guesses. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Randomized black-peg Codebreaker strategies use $O(n\log\log n+k)$ guesses for $k=\Omega(n)$ and $O(n\log(\log n/\log(n/k)))$ for $k=o(n)$.
assumptions: For Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k=k(n)$ colors
If $k= \Omega(n)$
If $k= o(n)$
conclusions: there exists a randomized winning strategy that uses black pegs only and needs an expected number of $O(n \log \log n + k)$ guesses
there exists a randomized winning strategy that uses black pegs only and needs an expected number of $O\left(n \log \left(\frac{\log n}{\log (n/k)}\right)\right)$ guesses
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Constants in Theorem 1 and the $\delta$ form of the bound
nodes.statement: The $O$-notation in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} only hides absolute constants. Note that, setting $k=:n^{1-\delta}$, $\delta=\delta(n)$, the bound for $k=o(n)$ translates to $O(n\log(\delta^{-1}))$.
nodes.statement_short: The O-notation hides only absolute constants; with $k=n^{1-\delta}$ the $k=o(n)$ bound is $O(n\log(1/\delta))$.

nodes.name: Zero-answer observation
nodes.statement: A simple but crucial observation is that when we query a string $x \in [k]^n$ and the answer $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$ is 0 (recall that $z$ denotes Codemaker's secret color code), then we know that all queried colors are wrong for their respective positions; i.e., we have $z_i\neq x_i$ for all $i \in [n]$.
nodes.statement_short: A $0$ answer to query $x$ shows that every queried color is wrong at its position.
assumptions: when we query a string $x \in [k]^n$ and the answer $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$  is 0
conclusions: we have $z_i\neq x_i$ for all $i \in [n]$

nodes.name: Candidate color sets $C_i$
nodes.statement: To make use of this observation, we maintain, for each position $i$, a set $C_i\subseteq[k]$ of colors that we still consider possible at position $i$.
differentia: that we still consider possible at position $i$

nodes.name: $0$-block
nodes.statement: We will refer to blocks that contribute $0$ to $\mathrm{eq}(z,r)$ as \emph{$0$-blocks} in the following.

nodes.name: Coin-weighing problem with a spring scale
nodes.statement: Specifically, we are given $m$ coins of unknown integer weights and a spring scale. We can use the spring scale to determine the total weight of an arbitrary subset of coins in one weighing. Our goal is to identify the weight of every coin with as few weighings as possible.
nodes.statement_short: Determine the integer weights of $m$ coins with as few subset-weighings on a spring scale as possible.

nodes.name: Heuristic phase count giving $O(n\log\log n)$
nodes.statement: Repeating this procedure of querying a random string $r$ and using additional `random coin-weighing queries' to identify the $0$-blocks eventually reduces the sizes of the sets $C_i$ below $k'/2$, at which point the phase ends. In total this requires $\Theta(k')$ rounds in which everything works out as sketched, corresponding to a total number of $\Theta(k'\cdot (m/\log m)) = \Theta(n / \log (4n/k'))$ queries for the entire phase. Summing over all phases, this suggests that for $k=n$ a total number of $$\sum_{j=1}^{\log k} O\left(\frac{n}{\log (4n/\left(\frac{k}{2^{j-1}} \right))}\right) \stackrel{k = n}= O(n) \sum_{j=1}^{\log n} \frac{1}{j+1} = O(n \log \log n) $$ queries suffice to determine the secret code $z$, as claimed in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} for $k=n$.
nodes.statement_short: Each phase needs $\Theta(k')$ rounds of $\Theta(m/\log m)$ queries; summing $n/\log(4n/k')$ over phases gives $O(n\log\log n)$ for $k=n$.

nodes.name: Deviation of Algorithm 1 from the sketch
nodes.statement: We remark that our precise strategy, Algorithm~\ref{algo:mastermind}, slightly deviates from this description. This is due to a technical issue with our argument once the number $k'$ of remaining colors drops below $C\log n$ for some $C>0$. Specifically, beyond this point the error bound we derive for a fixed position is not strong enough to beat a union bound over all $n$ positions. To avoid this issue, we stop our color reduction scheme before $k'$ becomes that small (for simplicity as soon as $k'$ is less than $\sqrt{n}$), and solve the remaining Mastermind problem by asking random queries from the remaining set $C_1\times \dots \times C_n$, as originally proposed by \ifLongCites{\cite{Erd63}}{Erd\H os and R\'enyi~\cite{Erd63}} and \ifLongCites{\cite{Chvatal83}}{Chv\'atal~\cite{Chvatal83}}.
nodes.statement_short: Color reduction stops once $k'<\sqrt n$ (union bound over positions fails for $k'=O(\log n)$); the rest is solved by random guessing.

nodes.name: Dummy color
nodes.statement: We begin by determining a dummy color for each position, i.e., a color that we know to be wrong at that particular position.
differentia: that we know to be wrong at that particular position

nodes.name: Dummy colors from $n+1$ queries
nodes.statement: For this we simply query the $n+1$ many strings $(1,1, \dots, 1), (2,1,1, \dots, 1), \dots, (2, 2, \dots, 2)\in [k]^n$. Processing the answers to these queries in order, it is not hard to determine the location of all $1$'s and $2$'s in Codemaker's secret string $z$. In particular, this provides us with a dummy color for each position.
nodes.statement_short: Querying the $n+1$ strings from $(1,\dots,1)$ to $(2,\dots,2)$ locates all 1s and 2s of $z$, giving a dummy color per position.
assumptions: we simply query  the $n+1$ many strings $(1,1, \dots, 1), (2,1,1, \dots, 1), \dots, (2, 2, \dots, 2)\in [k]^n$
conclusions: it is not hard to determine the location of all $1$'s and $2$'s in Codemaker's secret string $z$
this provides us with a dummy color for each position

nodes.name: WLOG $n$ and $k$ are powers of two
nodes.statement: Next we argue that for the main part of our argument we may assume that $n$ and $k$ are powers of two.
conclusions: we may assume that $n$ and $k$ are powers of two

nodes.name: Proof that $n$ and $k$ may be powers of two
nodes.statement: To see this for $n$, note that we can simply extend Codemaker's secret string in an arbitrary way such that its length is the smallest power of two larger than $n$, and pretend we are trying to determine this extended string. To get the answers to our queries in this extended setting, we just need to add the contribution of the self-made extension part (which we determine ourselves) to the answers Codemaker provides for the original string. As the extension changes $n$ at most by a factor of two, our claimed asymptotic bounds are unaffected by this. To argue that we may also assume $k$ to be a power of two, we make use of the dummy colors we already determined for the original value of $k$. Similar to the previous argument, we increase $k$ to the next power of two and consider the game with this larger number of colors. To get the answers to our queries in this extended setting from Codemaker (who still is in the original setting), it suffices to replace every occurrence of a color that is not in the original color set with the dummy color at the respective position.
nodes.statement_short: Padding argument: extend the secret string to a power-of-two length, and simulate extra colors by the dummy colors.

nodes.name: Padding $n$
nodes.statement: To see this for $n$, note that we can simply extend Codemaker's secret string in an arbitrary way such that its length is the smallest power of two larger than $n$, and pretend we are trying to determine this extended string. To get the answers to our queries in this extended setting, we just need to add the contribution of the self-made extension part (which we determine ourselves) to the answers Codemaker provides for the original string. As the extension changes $n$ at most by a factor of two, our claimed asymptotic bounds are unaffected by this.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the secret string to a power-of-two length and add the known contribution of the extension.

nodes.name: Padding $k$
nodes.statement: To argue that we may also assume $k$ to be a power of two, we make use of the dummy colors we already determined for the original value of $k$. Similar to the previous argument, we increase $k$ to the next power of two and consider the game with this larger number of colors. To get the answers to our queries in this extended setting from Codemaker (who still is in the original setting), it suffices to replace every occurrence of a color that is not in the original color set with the dummy color at the respective position.
nodes.statement_short: Increase $k$ to a power of two and replace new colors by dummy colors.

nodes.name: WLOG $k\le n$
nodes.statement: We may and will also assume that $k\leq n$.
conclusions: We may and will also assume that $k\leq n$.

nodes.name: Proof that we may assume $k\le n$
nodes.statement: If $k>n$ we can trivially reduce the number of colors to $n$ by making $k$ monochromatic queries.
nodes.statement_short: Monochromatic queries reduce the colors to at most $n$.

nodes.name: Phase
nodes.statement: As sketched above, our strategy operates in \emph{phases}, where in the $j$th phase we reduce the sizes of the sets $C_i$ from $k/2^{j-1}$ to $k/2^j$.
nodes.statement_short: Phase $j$ halves every $|C_i|$ from $k/2^{j-1}$ to $k/2^j$.

nodes.name: Round
nodes.statement: Each phase is divided into a large number of \emph{rounds}, where a round consists of querying a random string $r$ and subsequently identifying the $0$-blocks (blocks that contribute $0$ to $\mathrm{eq}(z,r)$) by the coin-weighing argument outlined above.
differentia: consists of querying a random string $r$ and subsequently identifying the $0$-blocks

nodes.name: Sampling set $\mathcal{R}_j$
nodes.statement: Specifically, at the beginning of phase $j$ we define the set ${\mathcal{R}}_j:=C_1\times \dots \times C_n$, and sample the random string $r$ uniformly at random from ${\mathcal{R}}_j$ in each round of phase $j$.

nodes.name: Block partition parameters $k'$ and $m$
nodes.statement: As before we let $k'~:=~k/2^{j-1}$ and partition the $n$ positions into $m := 4 n / k'$ blocks of size $k'/4$.
nodes.statement_short: With $k'=k/2^{j-1}$, split the $n$ positions into $m=4n/k'$ blocks of size $k'/4$.

nodes.name: Blocks $B_s$ and contributions $v_s$
nodes.statement: More formally, for every $s \in [m]$ we let $B_s := \{ (s-1) k'/4 +1, \dots, s k'/4 \}$ denote the indices of block $s$, and we denote by $v_s: = | \{ i \in B_s : z_i = r_i \} |$ the contribution of block $B_s$ to $\mathrm{eq}(z,r)$. (Note that $\sum_{s \in [m]} v_s = \mathrm{eq}(z,r)$.)
nodes.statement_short: $B_s$ is the $s$-th block of indices and $v_s$ its number of positions where $r$ matches $z$.

nodes.name: Coin-weighing query $r_y$

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement: We first show that a round is successful with probability at least $1/4$. Recall that $\mathrm{eq}(z,r)$ has an expected value of $n/k'=m/4$. Thus, by Markov's inequality, we have $\mathrm{eq}(z,r)\leq m/2$ with probability at least $1/2$. Moreover, as already mentioned, the proof of the coin-weighing result by \ifLongCites{\cite{grebinski-journal}}{Grebinski and Kucherov~\cite{grebinski-journal}} implies that our $f(m)=\Theta(m/\log m)$ random coin-weighing queries identify all $0$-blocks with probability at least $1/2$. Thus, in total the probability for a successful round is at least $1/2\cdot 1/2=1/4$. We continue by showing that the probability that a successful round decreases the number of available colors for a fixed position, say position 1, is at least $1/4$. Note that this happens if $r \in {\mathcal{R}}_j$ satisfies the following two conditions: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $v_1=0$, i.e., block $B_1$ is a 0-block with respect to $r$, and \item[(ii)] $r_1\in C_1$, i.e., the color $r_1$ has not been excluded from $C_1$ in a previous round of phase $j$. \end{itemize} For (i) recall that in a successful round at least $m/2$ of the $m$ blocks are $0$-blocks. It follows by symmetry that $B_1$ is a 0-block with probability at least $1/2$. Moreover, conditional on (i), $r_1$ is sampled uniformly at random from the $k'-1$ colors that are different from $z_1$ and were in $C_1$ at the beginning of the round. Thus the probability that $r_1$ is in the current set $C_1$ is $|C_1|/(k'-1)$, which is at least $1/2$ because we do not allow $|C_1|$ to drop below $k'/2$. We conclude that, conditional on a successful round, the random query $r$ decreases $|C_1|$ by one with probability at least $1/2\cdot 1/2=1/4$. Thus, in total, the probability that a round decreases $|C_1|$ by one is at least $1/4\cdot 1/4=1/16$ throughout our strategy. It follows that the probability that after $t$ successful rounds in phase $j$ we still have $|C_1|>k'/2$ is bounded by the probability that in $t$ independent Bernoulli trials with success probability $1/16$ we observe fewer than $k'/2$ successes. If $t/16\geq k'$, by Chernoff bounds this probability is bounded by $e^{-ct}$ for some absolute constant $c>0$. Let us now denote the number of rounds phase $j$ takes by the random variable $T$. By a union bound, the probability that $T\geq t$, i.e., that after $t$ steps at one of the positions $i\in[n]$ we still have $|C_i|>k'/2$, is bounded by $ne^{-ct}$ for $t\geq 16k'$. It follows that \begin{equation} \mathbb E[T] = \sum_{t \ge 1} \Pr[ T \ge t ] \le 16k' + n \sum_{t > 16k'} e^{-ct} = 16k' + n e^{-\Omega(k')}= O(k'), \end{equation} where the last step is due to $k'\geq \sqrt{n}=\omega(\log n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Probabilistic argument: a round succeeds w.p. $\ge1/4$ and then shrinks a fixed $C_i$ w.p. $\ge1/4$; Chernoff plus a union bound give $\mathbb E[T]=O(k')$.

nodes.statement: Recall that for each phase $j$ we have $m=\Theta(n/k')=\Theta(n/(k/2^{j-1}))$ and that $f(m)=\Theta(m/\log m)$. As the number of queries for determining the dummy colors and for wrapping up at the end is only $O(n)$, Theorem~\ref{thm:main} follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: The main loop of the algorithm described above uses randomization in two places: for generating the random string $r$ of each round (line~\ref{line:sample} in Algorithm 1), and for generating the $f(m)$ many random coin-weighing queries $r_y$ used to identify the $0$-blocks of $r$ if $\mathrm{eq}(z,r)\leq m/2$ (line~\ref{line:coins2}). The derandomization of the coin-weighing algorithm is already given in the work of \ifLongCites{\cite{grebinski-journal}}{Grebinski and Kucherov~\cite{grebinski-journal}}. They showed that a set of $f'(m)= \Theta(m/\log m)$ random coin-weighing queries $y^1, \ldots, y^{f'(m)}$, sampled from $\{0,1\}^m$ independently and uniformly at random, has, with some positive probability, the property that it distinguishes any two distinct coin-weighing instances in the following sense: For any two distinct vectors $v, w$ with non-negative integer entries such that $\sum_{s\in[m]}{v_s} \leq m/2$ and $\sum_{s\in[m]}{w_s} \leq m/2$, there exists an index $j\in[f'(m)]$ for which $\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{v_s}\neq\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{w_s}$. It follows by the probabilistic method that, deterministically, there is a set $D\subseteq \{0,1\}^m$ of size at most $f'(m)$ such that the answers to the corresponding coin-weighing queries identify every possible coin-weighing instance. Hence we can replace the $f(m)$ random coin-weighing queries of each round by the $f'(m)$ coin-weighing queries corresponding to the fixed set $D$. It remains to derandomize the choice of $r$ in each round. As before we consider $m:=4n/k'$ blocks of size $k'/4$, where $k'$ is the size of the sets $C_i$ at the beginning of a phase. To make sure that a constant fraction of all queries in a phase satisfy $\mathrm{eq}(z,r)\leq m/2$ (compare line~\ref{Bedingung} of Algorithm~\ref{algo:mastermind}), we ask a set of $k'$ queries such that, for each position $i\in[n]$, every color in $C_i$ is used at position $i$ in exactly one of these queries. (If all sets $C_i$ are equal, this can be achieved by simply asking $k'$ monochromatic queries.) The sum of all returned scores must be exactly $n$, and therefore we cannot get a score of more than $m/2 = 2n/k'$ for more than $k'/2$ queries. In this way we ensure that for at least $k-k'/2=k'/2$ queries we get a score of at most $m/2$. As in the randomized version of our strategy, in each of these $k'/2$ queries at least half of the blocks must be $0$-blocks. We can identify those by the derandomized coin-weighing discussed above. Consider now a fixed block. As it has size $k'/4$, it can be a \emph{non}-0-block in at most $k'/4$ queries. Thus it is a $0$-block in at least $k'/2-k'/4=k'/4$ of the queries. To summarize, we have shown that by asking $k'$ queries of the above form we get at least $k'/2$ queries of score at most $m/2$. For each of them we identify the $0$-blocks by coin-weighing queries. This allows us to exclude at least $k'/4$ colors at each position. I.e., as in the randomized version of our strategy we can reduce the number of colors by a constant factor using only $O(k'\cdot m/\log m)=O(n/\log(4n/k))$ queries. By similar calculations as before, the same asymptotic bounds follow. We abandon the color reduction scheme when $k'$ is a constant. At this point, we can solve the remaining problem in time $O(n)$ by repeatedly using the argument we used to determine the dummy colors in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}. Note that all of the above can easily be implemented in polynomial time if we can solve the coin-weighing subproblems in polynomial time. An algorithm for doing the latter is given in the work of \ifLongCites{\cite{Bshouty09}}{Bshouty~\cite{Bshouty09}}. Using this algorithm as a building block, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time strategy for Codebreaker that achieves the bounds stated in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
nodes.statement_short: Derandomize both random choices: a fixed coin-weighing set $D$ exists by the probabilistic method, and $k'$ color-covering queries replace random $r$. Bshouty's algorithm makes the coin weighing polynomial-time.

nodes.name: Grebinski-Kucherov distinguishing property
nodes.statement: The derandomization of the coin-weighing algorithm is already given in the work of \ifLongCites{\cite{grebinski-journal}}{Grebinski and Kucherov~\cite{grebinski-journal}}. They showed that a set of $f'(m)= \Theta(m/\log m)$ random coin-weighing queries $y^1, \ldots, y^{f'(m)}$, sampled from $\{0,1\}^m$ independently and uniformly at random, has, with some positive probability, the property that it distinguishes any two distinct coin-weighing instances in the following sense: For any two distinct vectors $v, w$ with non-negative integer entries such that $\sum_{s\in[m]}{v_s} \leq m/2$ and $\sum_{s\in[m]}{w_s} \leq m/2$, there exists an index $j\in[f'(m)]$ for which $\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{v_s}\neq\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{w_s}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall: $\Theta(m/\log m)$ random weighings distinguish all instances with positive probability.

nodes.name: Fixed coin-weighing set $D$
nodes.statement: It follows by the probabilistic method that, deterministically, there is a set $D\subseteq \{0,1\}^m$ of size at most $f'(m)$ such that the answers to the corresponding coin-weighing queries identify every possible coin-weighing instance. Hence we can replace the $f(m)$ random coin-weighing queries of each round by the $f'(m)$ coin-weighing queries corresponding to the fixed set $D$.
nodes.statement_short: Probabilistic method yields a fixed query set $D$ of size $f'(m)$.

nodes.name: Derandomize $r$
nodes.statement: It remains to derandomize the choice of $r$ in each round. As before we consider $m:=4n/k'$ blocks of size $k'/4$, where $k'$ is the size of the sets $C_i$ at the beginning of a phase. To make sure that a constant fraction of all queries in a phase satisfy $\mathrm{eq}(z,r)\leq m/2$ (compare line~\ref{Bedingung} of Algorithm~\ref{algo:mastermind}), we ask a set of $k'$ queries such that, for each position $i\in[n]$, every color in $C_i$ is used at position $i$ in exactly one of these queries. (If all sets $C_i$ are equal, this can be achieved by simply asking $k'$ monochromatic queries.) The sum of all returned scores must be exactly $n$, and therefore we cannot get a score of more than $m/2 = 2n/k'$ for more than $k'/2$ queries. In this way we ensure that for at least $k-k'/2=k'/2$ queries we get a score of at most $m/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $k'$ queries covering each color once per position; at least $k'/2$ have score $\le m/2$.

nodes.name: Each block is a 0-block often
nodes.statement: As in the randomized version of our strategy, in each of these $k'/2$ queries at least half of the blocks must be $0$-blocks. We can identify those by the derandomized coin-weighing discussed above. Consider now a fixed block. As it has size $k'/4$, it can be a \emph{non}-0-block in at most $k'/4$ queries. Thus it is a $0$-block in at least $k'/2-k'/4=k'/4$ of the queries.
nodes.statement_short: Each block is a $0$-block in at least $k'/4$ of these queries.

nodes.name: Phase cost
nodes.statement: To summarize, we have shown that by asking $k'$ queries of the above form we get at least $k'/2$ queries of score at most $m/2$. For each of them we identify the $0$-blocks by coin-weighing queries. This allows us to exclude at least $k'/4$ colors at each position. I.e., as in the randomized version of our strategy we can reduce the number of colors by a constant factor using only $O(k'\cdot m/\log m)=O(n/\log(4n/k))$ queries. By similar calculations as before, the same asymptotic bounds follow.
nodes.statement_short: Constant-factor color reduction per $O(n/\log(4n/k))$ queries gives the same bounds.

nodes.name: Wrap-up
nodes.statement: We abandon the color reduction scheme when $k'$ is a constant. At this point, we can solve the remaining problem in time $O(n)$ by repeatedly using the argument we used to determine the dummy colors in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}.
nodes.statement_short: Finish with the dummy-color argument in $O(n)$.

nodes.name: Polynomial time via Bshouty
nodes.statement: Note that all of the above can easily be implemented in polynomial time if we can solve the coin-weighing subproblems in polynomial time. An algorithm for doing the latter is given in the work of \ifLongCites{\cite{Bshouty09}}{Bshouty~\cite{Bshouty09}}. Using this algorithm as a building block, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time strategy for Codebreaker that achieves the bounds stated in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
nodes.statement_short: Bshouty's polynomial-time coin-weighing algorithm makes the strategy polynomial.

nodes.name: Three-step black/white strategy
nodes.statement: Codebreaker's strategy leading to the bound of Theorem~\ref{thmbw} consists of roughly these three steps. (1) Codebreaker first asks roughly $k/n$ guesses containing all colors. Only colors in a guess receiving a positive answer can be part of the secret code, so this reduces the number of colors to be regarded to at most $n^2$. Also, Codebreaker can learn from the answers the cardinality $n'$ of $C^*$, that is, the number of distinct colors in the secret code. (2) By asking an expected number of $\Theta(n')$ (dependent) random queries, Codebreaker learns $n'$ disjoint sets of colors of size at most $n$ such that each color of $C^*$ is contained in exactly one of these sets. Denote by $k'$ the cardinality of a largest of these sets. (3) Given such a family of sets, Codebreaker can learn $C^*$ with an expected number of $b(n', k')$ queries by simulating an optimal black-peg Mastermind strategy. Once $C^*$ is known, an expected number of $b(n,n')$ queries determine the secret code, using an optimal black-peg strategy for $n'$ colors.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, Codebreaker's strategy is to ask color queries having an expected answer of one. With constant probability, such a query contains exactly one color from $C^*$. Below is a precise formulation of this strategy. \begin{algorithm2e} \While{$n' > 0$}{ $k' \leftarrow \lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil$\; Let $C_{n'}$ be a random subset of $C$ with $|C_{n'}| = k'$\; Ask the color query $C_{n'}$\; \If{$\mathrm{col}(C_{n'}) = 1$}{ $C_0 \leftarrow C_0 \setminus C_{n'}$\; $n' \leftarrow n' - 1$\; } } \caption{Codebreaker's strategy} \end{algorithm2e} For the analysis, note first that the value of $k'$ during the application of the above strategy does not increase. In particular, all sets $C_i$ defined and queried have cardinality at most $\lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil \le n$. It is also clear that the above strategy constructs a sequence of disjoint $C_i$ and that for each color occurring in $z$ there is exactly one $C_i$ containing this color. It remains to prove the estimate on the expected number of queries. To this aim, we first note that throughout a run of this strategy, $n'$ is the number of colors of $C^*$ left in $C_0$. Hence the event ``$\mathrm{col}(C_{n'}) = 1$'' occurs with probability \begin{align*} \frac{n' k' (|C_0| - n') \ldots (|C_0| - n' - k' + 2)}{|C_0| \ldots (|C_0| - k' + 1)} &\ge \frac{(|C_0| - n') \ldots (|C_0| - n' - k' + 2)}{(|C_0|-1) \ldots (|C_0| - k' + 1)} \\ & \ge \bigg( \frac{|C_0| - n' - k' + 2}{|C_0| - k' + 1} \bigg)^{k'-1} = \bigg( 1 - \frac{n' - 1}{|C_0| - k' + 1} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{n' - 1}{|C_0| - (|C_0|/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{|C_0| / (k'-1)}{|C_0| - (|C_0|/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{1}{(k'-1)(1 - 1/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1},\\ \end{align*} which is bounded from below by a constant (the later estimates assume $n' \ge 2$; for $n'=1$ the second term of the sequence of inequalities already is one). Consequently, with constant probability the randomly chosen $C_{n'}$ satisfies ``$\mathrm{col}(C_{n'}) = 1$''. Hence after an expected constant number of iterations of the while-loop, such a $C_{n'}$ will be found. Since each such success reduces the value of $n'$ by one, a total expected number of $\Theta(|C^*|)$ iterations suffices to find the desired family of sets $(C_i)_{i \in [n']}$.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, Codebreaker's strategy is to ask color queries having an expected answer of one. With constant probability, such a query contains exactly one color from $C^*$. Below is a precise formulation of this strategy. \begin{algorithm2e} \While{$n' > 0$}{ $k' \leftarrow \lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil$\; Let $C_{n'}$ be a random subset of $C$ with $|C_{n'}| = k'$\; Ask the color query $C_{n'}$\; \If{$\mathrm{col}(C_{n'}) = 1$}{ $C_0 \leftarrow C_0 \setminus C_{n'}$\; $n' \leftarrow n' - 1$\; } } \caption{Codebreaker's strategy} \end{algorithm2e}

nodes.statement_short: Query random color sets with expected answer one (Algorithm 2).

nodes.name: Correctness
nodes.statement: For the analysis, note first that the value of $k'$ during the application of the above strategy does not increase. In particular, all sets $C_i$ defined and queried have cardinality at most $\lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil \le n$. It is also clear that the above strategy constructs a sequence of disjoint $C_i$ and that for each color occurring in $z$ there is exactly one $C_i$ containing this color.
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement_short: Set sizes stay $\le n$; the sets are disjoint and each holds one code color.

nodes.name: Success probability
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the estimate on the expected number of queries. To this aim, we first note that throughout a run of this strategy, $n'$ is the number of colors of $C^*$ left in $C_0$. Hence the event ``$\mathrm{col}(C_{n'}) = 1$'' occurs with probability \begin{align*} \frac{n' k' (|C_0| - n') \ldots (|C_0| - n' - k' + 2)}{|C_0| \ldots (|C_0| - k' + 1)} &\ge \frac{(|C_0| - n') \ldots (|C_0| - n' - k' + 2)}{(|C_0|-1) \ldots (|C_0| - k' + 1)} \\ & \ge \bigg( \frac{|C_0| - n' - k' + 2}{|C_0| - k' + 1} \bigg)^{k'-1} = \bigg( 1 - \frac{n' - 1}{|C_0| - k' + 1} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{n' - 1}{|C_0| - (|C_0|/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{|C_0| / (k'-1)}{|C_0| - (|C_0|/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{1}{(k'-1)(1 - 1/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1},\\ \end{align*} which is bounded from below by a constant (the later estimates assume $n' \ge 2$; for $n'=1$ the second term of the sequence of inequalities already is one).
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement_short: Probability that $\mathrm{col}(C_{n'})=1$ is bounded below by a constant.

nodes.name: Expected iterations
nodes.statement: Consequently, with constant probability the randomly chosen $C_{n'}$ satisfies ``$\mathrm{col}(C_{n'}) = 1$''. Hence after an expected constant number of iterations of the while-loop, such a $C_{n'}$ will be found. Since each such success reduces the value of $n'$ by one, a total expected number of $\Theta(|C^*|)$ iterations suffices to find the desired family of sets $(C_i)_{i \in [n']}$.

nodes.statement_short: Constant expected iterations per success give $\Theta(|C^*|)$ total.

Assume that $k' := \max\{|C_i| \mid i \in [n']\} \le n$. Then Codebreaker can detect $C^*$ using an expected number of $b(n', k')$ color queries.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement: Let $z' \in C_1 \times \ldots \times C_{n'}$ be the unique such string consisting of colors in $C^*$ only. Note that in black-peg Mastermind, the particular sets of colors used at each position are irrelevant. Hence there is a strategy for Codebreaker to detect $z'$ using an expected number of $b(n',k')$ guesses from $C_1 \times \ldots \times C_{n'}$ and receiving black-peg answers only. We now show that for each such query, there is a corresponding color query in the $(n,k)$ black/white Mastermind game giving the same answer. Hence we may simulate the black-peg game searching for $z'$ by such color queries. Since $z'$ contains all colors of $C^*$ and no other colors, once found, it reveals the set of colors occurring in the original secret code $z$. Let $y' \in C_1 \times \ldots \times C_{n'}$ be a query in the black-peg Mastermind game searching for $z'$. For each position $i\in[n']$, we have $z'_i=y'_i$ if and only if $y_i'\in C_i$ is the unique color from $C_i$ that is in $C^*$. As moreover the sets $(C_i)_{i\in [n']}$ are disjoint, we have $\mathrm{eq}(z',y') = \mathrm{col}(\{y'_1, \ldots, y'_{n'}\})$, and we can obtain this value (i.e., the black-peg answer for the guess $y'$ relative to $z'$) by a color query relative to $z$.

nodes.statement: Note that if our only goal is to find out $C^*$, then for $k \ll n^2$ we can be more efficient by asking more color queries in Lemma~\ref{lemreduce}, leading to a smaller set $C_0$, to smaller sets $C_i$ in Lemma~\ref{lempartition}, and thus to a smaller $k'$ value in Lemma~\ref{lemlast}. Since this will not affect the asymptotic bound for the total numbers of queries used in the black/white-peg game, we omit the details.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: The upper bound follows easily from applying Lemmas~\ref{lemfirst} to~\ref{lemlast}, which show that Codebreaker can detect the set $C^*$ of colors arising in the secret code $z$ with an expected number of $1 + \lceil k/n \rceil + O(n) + b(n,n)$ guesses. Since $|C^*| \le n$, he can now use a strategy for black-peg Mastermind and determine $z$ with another expected number of $b(n,n)$ guesses. Note that $b(n,n) = \Omega(n)$, so this proves the upper bound. We argue that this upper bound is optimal apart from constant factors. Assume first that the secret code is a random monochromatic string (Codemaker may even announce this). Fix a (possibly randomized) strategy for Codebreaker. With probability at least 1/2, this strategy does not use the particular color in any of the first $k/(2n)$ guesses. It then also did not guess the correct code. Hence the expected number of queries necessary to find the code is at least $k/(4n)$. We finally show that for $k \ge n$, also the $b(n,n)$ term cannot be avoided. By the information theoretic argument, there is nothing to show if $b(n,n) = \Theta(n)$. Hence assume $b(n,n) = \omega(n)$. We will show $bw(n,k) + n + 1 \ge bw(n,n)$. The claim then follows from $bw(n,n) = \Theta(b(n,n))$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:bw}). We show that we can solve the $k=n$ color Mastermind game by asking $n+1$ preliminary queries and then simulating a strategy for black/white Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k > n$. As in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}, we use $n+1$ queries to learn for each position whether it has color $1$ or not. We then simulate a given strategy for $k > n$ colors as follows. In a $k$-color query, replace all colors greater than $n$ by color $1$. Since we know the positions of the pegs in color $1$, we can reduce the answers by the contribution of these additional 1-pegs in the query. This gives the answer we would have gotten in reply to the original query (since the secret code does not contain colors higher than $n$). Consequently, we can now simulate the $k$-color strategy in an $n$-color Mastermind game.

nodes.name: Erdos-Renyi: random guessing for 2-color Mastermind
nodes.statement: In their work on the $2$-color black-peg version of Mastermind, \ifLongCites{\cite{Erd63}}{Erd{\H{o}}s and R\'enyi~\cite{Erd63}} showed that random guessing needs, with high probability, $(2+o(1)) n /\log n$ queries to identify the secret code, and that this is in fact best possible among \emph{non-adaptive} winning strategies.
assumptions: the $2$-color black-peg version of Mastermind
conclusions: random guessing needs, with high probability, $(2+o(1)) n /\log n$ queries to identify the secret code
this is in fact best possible among \emph{non-adaptive} winning strategies

nodes.name: Lindstrom / Cantor-Mills derandomization
nodes.statement: The upper bound was derandomized by \ifLongCites{\cite{Lindstroem64,Lindstroem65}}{Lindstr\"om~\cite{Lindstroem64,Lindstroem65}} and, independently, by \ifLongCites{\cite{CantorM66}}{Cantor and Mills~\cite{CantorM66}}. That is, for 2-color black-pegs Mastermind a deterministic non-adaptive winning strategy using $(2+o(1)) n /\log n$ guesses exists, and no non-adaptive strategy can do better.
assumptions: for 2-color black-pegs Mastermind
conclusions: a deterministic non-adaptive winning strategy using $(2+o(1)) n /\log n$ guesses exists

nodes.name: Optimal adaptive 2-color Mastermind
nodes.statement: It remains a major open problem whether there exists an adaptive strategy that achieves this bound. In fact, it is not even known whether adaptive strategies can outperform the random guessing strategy by \emph{any} constant factor.
nodes.statement_short: Can adaptive strategies attain $(1+o(1))n/\log n$, or even beat random guessing by a constant factor, for 2 colors?

nodes.name: Deterministic non-adaptive strategy
nodes.statement: A deterministic non-adaptive strategy is a fixed ordering $x^1, x^2, \ldots, x^{k^n}$ of all possible guesses, i.e., the elements of $[k]^n$.

nodes.name: Randomized non-adaptive strategy
nodes.statement: A randomized non-adaptive strategy is a probability distribution over such orderings.

nodes.name: Identification time of a non-adaptive strategy
nodes.statement: For a given secret code $z\in[k]^n$, we ask for the smallest index $j$ such that the queries $x^1, \ldots, x^j$ together with their answers $\mathrm{eq}(z,x^1), \ldots, \mathrm{eq}(z,x^j)$ uniquely determine $z$.

nodes.name: Lower bound for non-adaptive strategies
nodes.statement: For any (randomized or deterministic) non-adaptive strategy for black-peg Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k$ colors, the expected number of queries needed to determine a secret code $z$ sampled uniformly at random from $[k]^n$ is $\Omega \left( \frac{n \log k}{\max\{\log(n/k), 1\}} \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Any non-adaptive strategy needs $\Omega(n\log k/\max\{\log(n/k),1\})$ expected queries on a uniform random code.
assumptions: For any (randomized or deterministic) non-adaptive strategy for black-peg Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k$ colors
a secret code $z$ sampled uniformly at random from $[k]^n$
conclusions: $\Omega \left( \frac{n \log k}{\max\{\log(n/k), 1\}} \right)$
nodes.label: thm:nonadaptive

nodes.name: Worst-case form of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:nonadaptive} shows, in particular, that for any non-adaptive strategy there exists a secret code $z\in[k]^n$ which can only be identified after $\Omega\left(n \log k / \max\{\log(n/k), 1\} \right)$ queries. For $k\geq n$, this is an improvement of $\Theta(\log n)$ over the information-theoretic lower bound mentioned in the introduction.
nodes.statement_short: Some code needs $\Omega(n\log k/\max\{\log(n/k),1\})$ queries; for $k\ge n$ this beats the information-theoretic bound by $\Theta(\log n)$.

nodes.name: Adaptive beats non-adaptive for $k=\Theta(n)$
nodes.statement: For the case $k=\Theta(n)$ Theorem~\ref{thm:nonadaptive} gives a lower bound of $\Omega(n \log n)$ guesses for every non-adaptive strategy, showing that adaptive strategies are indeed more powerful than non-adaptive ones in this regime (recall Theorem~\ref{thm:main}).

nodes.name: Information-gain intuition for Theorem 11
nodes.statement: To give an intuition for the correctness of Theorem~\ref{thm:nonadaptive}, note that for a uniformly chosen secret code $z \in [k]^n$, for any single fixed guess $x$ of a non-adaptive strategy the answer $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$ is binomially distributed with parameters $n$ and $1/k$. That is, $\mathrm{eq}(z,x)$ will typically be within the interval $n/k \pm O(\sqrt{n/k})$. Hence, we can typically encode the answer using $\log( O(\sqrt{n/k})) = O(\log(n/k))$ bits. Or, stated differently, our `information gain' is usually $O(\log(n/k))$ bits. Since the secret code `holds $n \log k$ bits of information', we would expect that we have to make $\Omega(n \log k / \log(n/k))$ guesses.
nodes.statement_short: Each answer is Binomial$(n,1/k)$ and carries $O(\log(n/k))$ bits while the code has $n\log k$ bits.

nodes.name: Entropy
nodes.statement: For a discrete random variable $Z$ over a domain $D$, the \emph{entropy} of $Z$ is defined by $H(Z) := - \sum_{z \in D} \Pr[Z = z] \log(\Pr[Z=z])$.

nodes.name: Entropy of a function (E1)
nodes.statement: If $Z$ is determined by the outcome of $Y$, i.e., $Z = f(Y)$ for a deterministic function $f$, then we have $H(Z) \le H(Y)$.
assumptions: If $Z$ is determined by the outcome of $Y$, i.e., $Z = f(Y)$ for a deterministic function $f$
conclusions: $H(Z) \le H(Y)$

nodes.name: Subadditivity of entropy (E2)
nodes.statement: We have $H((Z, Y)) \le H(Z) + H(Y)$.
conclusions: $H((Z, Y)) \le H(Z) + H(Y)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 12
nodes.statement: We can easily eliminate colors whenever we receive a $0$-answer. For every position $i \in [n]$ we need to eliminate $k-1$ potential colors. This can be seen as having $n$ parallel coupon collectors, each of which needs to collect $k-1$ coupons. The probability that for a random guess we get an answer of $0$ is $(1-1/k)^n$, i.e., constant. Conditional on a $0$-answer, the color excluded at each position is sampled uniformly from all $k-1$ colors that are wrong at that particular position. Thus the probability that at least one of the $k-1$ wrong colors at one fixed position is \emph{not} eliminated by the first $t$ $0$-answers is bounded by $(k-1)(1-\frac{1}{k-1})^t\leq k e^{-t/k}$. Let now $T$ denote the random variable that counts the number of $0$-answers needed to determine the secret code. By a union bound over all $n$ positions, we have $\Pr[T\geq t]\leq nk\textup{e}^{-t/k}=\Theta(n^2)\cdot e^{-\Theta(t/n)}$. It follows by routine calculations that $\mathbb{E}[T]=O(n\log n)$ and $\Pr[T\geq Cn\log n]=o(1)$ for $C$ large enough. As a random query returns a value of $0$ with constant probability, the same bounds also hold for the total number of queries needed.

Hence, the bound claimed in Theorem~ef{thm:non-adaptive-lb} evaluates to $O(n \log n)$ in this case. It thus suffices to show that there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that $N = C n \log n$ queries already identify every secret code with high probability. nodes.statement:
If a set $X=\{x^{(i)} \mid i \in N\}$ of queries distinguishes any two possible secret codes $z, z'$, then there must exist for each such pair $z
eq z'$ a query $x \in X$ with $\mathrm{eq}(z,x) 
eq \mathrm{eq}(z',x)$. In particular we must have $| \{ i \in I(z,z') : x_i = z_i \} | 
eq | \{ i \in I(z,z') : x_i = z'_i \} |$ for $I(z,z') := \{ i \in [n] : z_i 
eq z'_i \}$.
nodes.statement_short: A distinguishing query must treat differing positions unequally.

nodes.name: Difference pattern
nodes.statement: Based on this observation we define (similar to~\cite{Chvatal83}) a \emph{difference pattern} to be a set of indices $I \subseteq [n]$ together with two lists of colors $(c_i)_{i \in I}, (c'_i)_{i \in I}$ such that $c_i \neq c'_i$ for every $i \in I$.
nodes.statement_short: Define difference patterns.

nodes.name: Pattern of two codes
nodes.statement: For every two distinct secret codes $z, z' \in [k]^n$ we define the difference pattern corresponding to $z$ and $z'$ to be the set $I(z,z') := \{ i \in [n] : z_i \neq z'_i \}$ together with the lists $(z_i)_{i \in I}$ and $(z'_i)_{i \in I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Associate a difference pattern to each pair of codes.

nodes.name: Splitting
nodes.statement: We say that a query $x \in [k]^n$ \emph{splits} a difference pattern given by $I$, $(c_i)_{i \in I}$, and $(c'_i)_{i \in I}$ if \[ | \{ i \in I : x_i = c_i \} | \neq | \{ i \in I : x_i = c'_i \} |. \] It is now easy to see that if a set of $N$ queries has the property that every possible difference pattern is split by at least one query from that set, then these $N$ queries together with the answers deterministically identify Codebreaker's secret code.
nodes.statement_short: Splitting all patterns suffices to identify every code.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: In the following we show that a set of $N = C \frac{n \log k}{\max \{ \log(n/k), 1 \}}$ random queries with probability at least $1 - 1/n$ has the property that it splits every difference pattern.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: $N$ random queries split every pattern w.p. $\ge1-1/n$.

nodes.name: Union bound over sizes
nodes.statement: The \emph{size} of a difference pattern $I$, $(c_i)_{i \in I}$, $(c'_i)_{i \in I}$ is the cardinality of $I$. Note that for fixed $k$, the probability that a particular difference pattern is \emph{not} split by a randomly chosen query only depends on its size. Let $p(d,k)$ denote this probability for a difference pattern of size $d$. The probability that there exists a difference pattern that is not split by any of the $N$ random queries is at most \[ \sum_{d=1}^{n} \binom nd (k(k-1))^d (p(d,k))^N . \] In order to show that this probability is at most $1/n$ it thus suffices to prove that for every $d \in [n]$ we have \begin{equation} \binom nd (k(k-1))^d (p(d,k))^N < n^{-2} . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Union bound reduces to inequality (5) for every $d$.

nodes.name: Bounding $p(d,k)$
nodes.statement: We first take a closer look at $p(d,k)$. Observe that if a query $x$ does \emph{not} split a fixed difference pattern $I$, $(c_i)_{i \in I}$, $(c'_i)_{i \in I}$, then $x_i$ must agree with $c_i$ on exactly half of the positions in $I':=\{ i \in I \mid x_i \in \{c_i,c'_i\} \}$, and it must agree with $c'_i$ on the other positions in $I'$. In particular, the size of $I'$ must be even. More precisely, we have \begin{align*} p(d,k) & = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor d/2 \rfloor} \binom d{2i} \binom{2i}i \left( \frac 1k \right)^{2i} \left(1 - \frac2k \right)^{d-2i} \\ & = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor d/2 \rfloor} \binom d{2i} \left( \frac 2k \right)^{2i} \left(1 - \frac2k \right)^{d-2i} \binom{2i}{i} 2^{-2i} . \end{align*} Note that $\binom{2i}i 2^{-2i} \le 1/2$ for every $i \ge 1$, and $1-x \leq e^{-x}$ for all $x\in {\mathbb{R}}$. Hence, \begin{align*} p(d,k) & \le \left( 1 - \frac 2k \right)^d + \frac12 \sum_{j=1}^{d} \binom dj \left( \frac2k \right)^{j} \left( 1 - \frac2k \right)^{d-j} \\ & = 1 - \frac12 \left(1 - \left(1 - \frac2k \right)^d \right) \\ & \le \exp \left( - \frac12 \left(1 - e^{- \frac{2d}{k}} \right) \right). \end{align*} It follows that \begin{equation} \ln \frac 1{p(d,k)} \ge \frac12 \left( 1 - e^{- \frac{2d}{k}} \right) . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Exact formula for $p(d,k)$ and the bound (6).

nodes.name: Case split on $k$
nodes.statement: We now split the proof into two cases, $k \ge cn$ and $k < cn$ where $c$ is a sufficiently small constant. (We determine $c$ at the end of the proof.)
nodes.statement_short: Split into $k\ge cn$ and $k<cn$.

nodes.name: Case 1: $k\ge cn$
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 1.} $k \ge c n$. Observe that in this case $\log(n/k) \le \log(1/c)$ and $\log k = \log n + \Theta(1)$. Hence, the bound claimed in Theorem~\ref{thm:non-adaptive-lb} evaluates to $O(n \log n)$ in this case. It thus suffices to show that there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that $N = C n \log n$ queries already identify every secret code with high probability. We show $n^{5d}(p(d,k))^N < 1$ for every $d \in [n]$, which clearly implies~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-ultimate-goal}. In fact, we show the equivalent inequality \begin{equation} \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} > \ln n. \end{equation} Using~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-pdk} we obtain \begin{equation} \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge \frac{N}{10} \frac{1-e^{-\frac{2d}{k}}}{d}. \end{equation} Using that $d \mapsto (1-e^{-2d/k})/d$ is a decreasing function in $d$ we can continue with \[ \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge \frac{N}{10} \frac{(1-e^{-\frac{2n}{k}})}{n}, \] which is clearly larger than $\ln n$ for any $N > \frac{10}{(1-e^{-2}) \log e} n \log n$. Hence for such $N$ we have~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1} which settles this case.
nodes.statement_short: For $k\ge cn$ show (7) for all $d$, using monotonicity of $(1-e^{-2d/k})/d$.

nodes.name: Case 1 parameters
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 1.} $k \ge c n$. Observe that in this case $\log(n/k) \le \log(1/c)$ and $\log k = \log n + \Theta(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Here $\log(n/k)=O(1)$ and $\log k=\log n+\Theta(1)$.

nodes.name: Case 1 target
nodes.statement: Hence, the bound claimed in Theorem~\ref{thm:non-adaptive-lb} evaluates to $O(n \log n)$ in this case. It thus suffices to show that there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that $N = C n \log n$ queries already identify every secret code with high probability.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices that $N=Cn\log n$ queries work.

nodes.name: Case 1 estimate
nodes.statement: We show $n^{5d}(p(d,k))^N < 1$ for every $d \in [n]$, which clearly implies~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-ultimate-goal}. In fact, we show the equivalent inequality \begin{equation} \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} > \ln n. \end{equation} Using~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-pdk} we obtain \begin{equation} \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge \frac{N}{10} \frac{1-e^{-\frac{2d}{k}}}{d}. \end{equation} Using that $d \mapsto (1-e^{-2d/k})/d$ is a decreasing function in $d$ we can continue with \[ \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge \frac{N}{10} \frac{(1-e^{-\frac{2n}{k}})}{n}, \] which is clearly larger than $\ln n$ for any $N > \frac{10}{(1-e^{-2}) \log e} n \log n$. Hence for such $N$ we have~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1} which settles this case.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (7) via (6) and monotonicity in $d$.

nodes.name: Case 2: $k<cn$
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 2.} $k < c n$. In this case we need to be more careful in our analysis since in our claimed bound the factor $\log(n/k)$ might be large and the factor $\log k$ might be substantially smaller than $\log n$. In what follows, we regard only the case $k \ge 3$; the case $k=2$ has already been solved, cf.~\cite{Erd63}. We first consider difference patterns of size $d \le \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$. As in Case 1 we show that~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1} holds for these patterns. Observe that~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1-step1} holds again in this case. Since the function $d \mapsto (1-e^{-2d/k})/d$ is decreasing in $d$ and since $d \le \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$ we obtain \begin{equation} \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge \frac{N}{10} \frac{(1-e^{-\frac{2n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}}) \log(n/k) \log n}{n \log k}. \end{equation} Next we bound the exponent $\frac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ in the previous expression. Note that the derivative of $\frac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ with respect to $k$ is \begin{equation} \frac{ n ( \log n - \ln(2) \log k \log (n/k))}{\ln(2) k^2 \log n \log^2(n/k)}. \end{equation} We now show that this expression is less than 0 for $3 \le k \le n/4$. Indeed, observe that by setting $g(k) = \ln(2) \log k \log(n/k)$ we have for $n$ large enough that $g(3) = \ln(2) \log(3) \log (n/3) > 1.09 \log(n) - 3.3 > \log n$ and $g(n/4) = 2\ln(2) \log(n/4)>\log n$. Moreover, observe that \[ g'(k) = \frac{\log n - \log(k^2)}{k}. \] From this one easily sees that the function $g$ has a local maximum at $k=\sqrt{n}$ as its only extremal point in the interval in the interval $3 \le k \le n/4$. Hence $g(k) > \log n$ for every $3 \le k \le n/4$ and thus \eqref{eq:non-adaptive-exponent} is negative. Hence, $\frac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ is a decreasing function in $k$ and we have $\frac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n} \ge \frac{1}{c \log(1/c)} \left(1 + \frac{\log c}{\log n} \right) \ge 1$ for $n$ large enough. With this we can continue~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-continue-bla} with \[ \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge \frac{1-e^{-2}}{10} \frac{N \log(n/k) \log n}{n \log k}, \] which is certainly larger than $\ln n$ for any $N \ge \frac{10}{(1-e^{-2}) \log e} \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k)}$. This settles the case $k<cn$ for all $d \le \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$. In the remainder of this proof we consider the case $k<cn$ and $d \ge \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$. For such $d$ we establish the inequality $2^n k^{2n} (p(d,k))^N < n^{-2}$ which clearly implies~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-ultimate-goal}. As done previously, we actually show the equivalent inequality \begin{equation} N \log \frac1{p(d,k)} > 2 n \log k + n + 2 \log n. \end{equation} First observe that $\binom{2i}{i} 2^{-2i} \le 1/\sqrt{i}$ for every $i \ge 1$. We denote by $\mathcal Bin(n,p)$ a binomially dsitributed random variable with parameters $n$ and $p$. With this, we obtain \begin{align*} p(d,k) & \le \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor d/k \rfloor} \binom dj \left( \frac 2k \right)^j \left( 1 - \frac 2k \right)^{d-j} + \left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2} \sum_{j = \lfloor d/k \rfloor + 1}^{n} \binom dj \left( \frac 2k \right)^j \left( 1 - \frac 2k \right)^{d-j} \\ & = \Pr \left[ \mathcal Bin \left( d,\frac 2k \right) \le \frac{d}{k} \right] + \left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2} \sum_{j = \lfloor d/k \rfloor + 1}^{n} \binom dj \left( \frac 2k \right)^j \left( 1 - \frac 2k \right)^{d-j} . \end{align*} Using the Chernoff bound $\Pr[ \mathcal Bin(n,p) \le (1 - \delta) np] \le \left( \frac{e^{-\delta}}{(1-\delta)^{1-\delta}}\right)^{np}$ we obtain \[ \Pr \left[ \mathcal Bin \left( d,\frac 2k \right) \le \frac{d}{k} \right] \le \left( \frac{e^{-1/2}}{\left( 1/2 \right)^{1/2}} \right)^{2d/k} = \left( \frac 2e \right)^{d/k}. \] Hence, we have \[ p(d,k) \le \left( \frac 2e \right)^{d/k} + \left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2} . \] It is not hard to see that the function \[ f(k) = \frac{\left( \frac2e \right)^{d/k}}{\left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2}} \] attains its maximum at $k = 2(1 - \ln 2)d$ and that $f(2(1-\ln 2)d) \le 1$. Hence we have \[ p(d,k) \le 2 \left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2} = \left( \frac{d}{4k} \right)^{-1/2}. \] With this we obtain \begin{align*} N \log \frac 1{p(d,k)} & \ge \frac N2 ( \log d - \log k - 2) \\ & \ge \frac N2 ( \log n + \log \log k - \log \log (n/k) - \log \log n - \log k - 2) \\ & = \frac N2 ( \log(n/k) - \log \log (n/k) - \log \left( \frac{\log n}{\log k} \right) - 2 ) \\ & \ge \frac N4 \log(n/k) \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from $\frac12 \log(n/k) - \log \log (n/k) - \log( \frac{\log n}{\log k} ) - 2 \ge 0$ for every $k \le cn$ for a sufficiently small constant $c > 0$ and $n$ large enough. (In fact, this step imposes the most restrictive bound on $c$, i.e., any $c > 0$ that, for $n$ large enough, satisfies $\frac12 \log(1/c) - \log \log (1/c) - \log( 1 - \frac{\log c}{\log cn}) - 2 \ge 0$ is appropriate for our proof.) Clearly $\frac N4 \log(n/k)$ is larger than $2n \log k + n + 2 \log n$ for any $N > 16 \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k)}$ and $n$ large enough. This implies~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case2b} and thus settles this last case.
nodes.statement_short: For $k<cn$ treat small and large difference patterns separately.

nodes.name: Case 2 caution
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 2.} $k < c n$. In this case we need to be more careful in our analysis since in our claimed bound the factor $\log(n/k)$ might be large and the factor $\log k$ might be substantially smaller than $\log n$.
nodes.statement_short: The bound needs more care when $k$ is small.

nodes.name: Exclude $k=2$
nodes.statement: In what follows, we regard only the case $k \ge 3$; the case $k=2$ has already been solved, cf.~\cite{Erd63}.
nodes.statement_short: The case $k=2$ is Erdos-Renyi.

nodes.name: Small patterns
nodes.statement: We first consider difference patterns of size $d \le \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$. As in Case 1 we show that~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1} holds for these patterns. Observe that~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1-step1} holds again in this case. Since the function $d \mapsto (1-e^{-2d/k})/d$ is decreasing in $d$ and since $d \le \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$ we obtain \begin{equation} \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge \frac{N}{10} \frac{(1-e^{-\frac{2n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}}) \log(n/k) \log n}{n \log k}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For small $d$, monotonicity gives (9).

nodes.name: Derivative of exponent
nodes.statement: Next we bound the exponent $\frac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ in the previous expression. Note that the derivative of $\frac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ with respect to $k$ is \begin{equation} \frac{ n ( \log n - \ln(2) \log k \log (n/k))}{\ln(2) k^2 \log n \log^2(n/k)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compute the derivative (10) in $k$.

nodes.name: Sign of derivative
nodes.statement: We now show that this expression is less than 0 for $3 \le k \le n/4$. Indeed, observe that by setting $g(k) = \ln(2) \log k \log(n/k)$ we have for $n$ large enough that $g(3) = \ln(2) \log(3) \log (n/3) > 1.09 \log(n) - 3.3 > \log n$ and $g(n/4) = 2\ln(2) \log(n/4)>\log n$. Moreover, observe that \[ g'(k) = \frac{\log n - \log(k^2)}{k}. \] From this one easily sees that the function $g$ has a local maximum at $k=\sqrt{n}$ as its only extremal point in the interval in the interval $3 \le k \le n/4$.
nodes.statement_short: $g(k)=\ln 2\log k\log(n/k)$ exceeds $\log n$ at the endpoints and has a single maximum.

nodes.name: Derivative negative
nodes.statement: Hence $g(k) > \log n$ for every $3 \le k \le n/4$ and thus \eqref{eq:non-adaptive-exponent} is negative.
nodes.statement_short: So (10) is negative.

nodes.name: Small patterns settled
nodes.statement: Hence, $\frac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ is a decreasing function in $k$ and we have $\frac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n} \ge \frac{1}{c \log(1/c)} \left(1 + \frac{\log c}{\log n} \right) \ge 1$ for $n$ large enough. With this we can continue~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-continue-bla} with \[ \frac{N}{5d} \ln \frac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge \frac{1-e^{-2}}{10} \frac{N \log(n/k) \log n}{n \log k}, \] which is certainly larger than $\ln n$ for any $N \ge \frac{10}{(1-e^{-2}) \log e} \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k)}$. This settles the case $k<cn$ for all $d \le \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Decreasing exponent gives (7) for small $d$ when $N\gtrsim n\log k/\log(n/k)$.

nodes.name: Large patterns target
nodes.statement: In the remainder of this proof we consider the case $k<cn$ and $d \ge \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$. For such $d$ we establish the inequality $2^n k^{2n} (p(d,k))^N < n^{-2}$ which clearly implies~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-ultimate-goal}. As done previously, we actually show the equivalent inequality \begin{equation} N \log \frac1{p(d,k)} > 2 n \log k + n + 2 \log n. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For large $d$ it suffices to show (11).

nodes.name: Large patterns estimate
nodes.statement: First observe that $\binom{2i}{i} 2^{-2i} \le 1/\sqrt{i}$ for every $i \ge 1$. We denote by $\mathcal Bin(n,p)$ a binomially dsitributed random variable with parameters $n$ and $p$. With this, we obtain \begin{align*} p(d,k) & \le \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor d/k \rfloor} \binom dj \left( \frac 2k \right)^j \left( 1 - \frac 2k \right)^{d-j} + \left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2} \sum_{j = \lfloor d/k \rfloor + 1}^{n} \binom dj \left( \frac 2k \right)^j \left( 1 - \frac 2k \right)^{d-j} \\ & = \Pr \left[ \mathcal Bin \left( d,\frac 2k \right) \le \frac{d}{k} \right] + \left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2} \sum_{j = \lfloor d/k \rfloor + 1}^{n} \binom dj \left( \frac 2k \right)^j \left( 1 - \frac 2k \right)^{d-j} . \end{align*} Using the Chernoff bound $\Pr[ \mathcal Bin(n,p) \le (1 - \delta) np] \le \left( \frac{e^{-\delta}}{(1-\delta)^{1-\delta}}\right)^{np}$ we obtain \[ \Pr \left[ \mathcal Bin \left( d,\frac 2k \right) \le \frac{d}{k} \right] \le \left( \frac{e^{-1/2}}{\left( 1/2 \right)^{1/2}} \right)^{2d/k} = \left( \frac 2e \right)^{d/k}. \] Hence, we have \[ p(d,k) \le \left( \frac 2e \right)^{d/k} + \left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2} . \] It is not hard to see that the function \[ f(k) = \frac{\left( \frac2e \right)^{d/k}}{\left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2}} \] attains its maximum at $k = 2(1 - \ln 2)d$ and that $f(2(1-\ln 2)d) \le 1$. Hence we have \[ p(d,k) \le 2 \left( \frac dk \right)^{-1/2} = \left( \frac{d}{4k} \right)^{-1/2}. \] With this we obtain \begin{align*} N \log \frac 1{p(d,k)} & \ge \frac N2 ( \log d - \log k - 2) \\ & \ge \frac N2 ( \log n + \log \log k - \log \log (n/k) - \log \log n - \log k - 2) \\ & = \frac N2 ( \log(n/k) - \log \log (n/k) - \log \left( \frac{\log n}{\log k} \right) - 2 ) \\ & \ge \frac N4 \log(n/k) \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from $\frac12 \log(n/k) - \log \log (n/k) - \log( \frac{\log n}{\log k} ) - 2 \ge 0$ for every $k \le cn$ for a sufficiently small constant $c > 0$ and $n$ large enough. (In fact, this step imposes the most restrictive bound on $c$, i.e., any $c > 0$ that, for $n$ large enough, satisfies $\frac12 \log(1/c) - \log \log (1/c) - \log( 1 - \frac{\log c}{\log cn}) - 2 \ge 0$ is appropriate for our proof.) Clearly $\frac N4 \log(n/k)$ is larger than $2n \log k + n + 2 \log n$ for any $N > 16 \frac{n \log k}{\log(n/k)}$ and $n$ large enough. This implies~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case2b} and thus settles this last case.
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff gives $p(d,k)\le(d/4k)^{-1/2}$, hence $N\log(1/p)\ge\frac N4\log(n/k)$ and (11).
